source_text: Ὡς δὲ οἱ πολλοὶ ἄνθρωποι οἱ καθέλκοντες τὴν ναῦν οὐ πολλὰ αἴτια λέγοιντ’ ἄν, ἀλλ’ ἐκ πολλῶν αἴτιον ἕν (οὐκ ἔστι γὰρ αἴτιος ἕκαστος τοῦ καθέλκεσθαι τὴν ναῦν, ἀλλὰ σὺν τοῖς ἄλλοις), οὕτω καὶ ἡ φιλοσοφία πρὸς κατάληψιν τῆς ἀληθείας, ζήτησις οὖσα ἀληθείας, συλλαμβάνεται, οὐκ αἰτία οὖσα καταλήψεως, σὺν δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις αἰτία καὶ συνεργός. τάχα δὲ καὶ τὸ συναίτιον αἴτιον. ὡς δὲ, ἑνὸς ὄντος τοῦ εὐδαιμονεῖν, αἴτιαι τυγχάνουσιν αἱ ἀρεταὶ πλείονες ὑπάρχουσαι. καὶ ὡς τοῦ θερμαίνεσθαι ὅ τε ἥλιος τό τε πῦρ βαλανεῖόν τε καὶ ἐσθής, οὕτω μιᾶς οὔσης τῆς ἀληθείας πολλὰ τὰ συλλαμβανόμενα πρὸς ζήτησιν αὐτῆς, ἡ δὲ εὕρεσις δἰ υἱοῦ. εἰ γοῦν σκοποῖμεν, μία κατὰ δύναμίν ἐστιν ἡ ἀρετή, ταύτην δὲ συμβέβηκεν τούτοις μὲν τοῖς πράγμασιν ἐγγενομένην λέγεσθαι φρόνησιν, ἐν τούτοις δὲ σωφροσύνην, ἐν τούτοις δὲ ἀνδρείαν ἢ δικαιοσύνην. ἀνὰ τὸν αὐτὸν οὖν λόγον, καὶ μιᾶς οὔσης ἀληθείας, ἐν γεωμετρίᾳ μὲν γεωμετρίας ἀλήθεια, ἐν μουσικῇ δὲ μουσικῆς, κἀν φιλοσοφίᾳ τῇ ὀρθῇ Ἑλληνικὴ εἴη ἂν ἀλήθεια. μόνη δὲ ἡ κυρία αὕτη ἀλήθεια ἀπαρεγχείρητος, ἢν παρὰ τῷ υἱῷ τοῦ θεοῦ παιδευόμεθα. τοῦτόν φαμεν τὸν τρόπον μιᾶς καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς δραχμῆς τῷ μὲν ναυκλήρῳ δοθείσης λέγεσθαι ναῦλον, τῷ δὲ τελώνῃ τέλος καὶ ἐνοίκιον μὲν τῶ σταθμούχῳ, μισθὸν δὲ τῷ διδασκάλῳ καὶ τῶ πιπράσκοντι ἀρραβῶνα. ἑκάστη δὲ εἴτε ἀρετὴ εἴτε καὶ ἀλήθεια συνωνύμως καλουμένη μόνου τοῦ καθ’ ἑαυτὴν ἀποτελέσματός ἐστιν αἰτία. κατὰ σύγχρησιν δὲ τούτων γίνεται τὸ εὐδαιμόνως ζῆν (μὴ γὰρ δὴ εὐδαιμονῶμεν πρὸς τὰ ὀνόματα), ὅταν τὸν ὀρθὸν βίον εὐδαιμονίαν λέγωμεν καὶ εὐδαίμονα τὸν κεκοσμημένον τὴν ψυχὴν ἐναρέτως. εἰ δὲ καὶ πόρρωθεν συλλαμβάνεται φιλοσοφία πρὸς τὴν ἀληθείας εὕρεσιν, κατὰ διαφόρους ἐπιβολὰς διατείνουσα ἐπὶ τὴν προσεχῶς ἁπτομένην τῆς ἀληθείας τὴν καθ’ ἡμᾶς εἴδησιν, ἀλλὰ συλλαμβάνεταί γε τῶ λογικῶς ἐπιχειρεῖν ἐσπουδακότι ἀνθάπτεσθαι γνώσεως. χωρίζεται δὲ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ ἀλήθεια τῆς καθ’ ἡμᾶς, εἰ καὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ μετείληφεν ὀνόματος. καὶ μεγέθει γνώσεως καὶ ἀποδείξει κυριωτέρᾳ καὶ θεία δυνάμει καὶ τοῖς ὁμοίοις· θεοδίδακτοι γὰρ ἡμεῖς, ἱερὰ ὄντως, γράμματα παρὰ τῷ υἱῷ τοῦ θεοῦ παιδευόμενοι· ἔνθεν οὐδ’ ὡσαύτως κινοῦσι τὰς ψυχάς, ἀλλὰ διαφόρῳ διδασκαλίᾳ. εἰ δὲ καὶ διαστέλλεσθαι ἡμᾶς διὰ τοὺς φιλεγκλήμονας δεήσει, συναίτιον τὴν φιλοσοφίαν καὶ συνεργὸν λέγοντες τῆς ἀληθοῦς καταλήψεως, ζήτησιν οὖσαν ἀληθείας, προπαιδείαν αὐτὴν ὁμολογήσομεν τοῦ γνωστικοῦ οὐκ αἴτιον τιθέμενοι τὸ συναίτιον οὐδὲ μὴν τὸ συνεργὸν συνεκτικὸν οὐδ’ ὡς οὗ οὐκ ἄνευ τὴν φιλοσοφίαν, ἐπεὶ σχεδὸν οἱ πάντες ἄνευ τῆς ἐγκυκλίου παιδείας καὶ φιλοσοφίας τῆς Ἑλληνικῆς, οἳ δὲ καὶ ἄνευ γραμμάτων, τῇ θείᾳ καὶ βαρβάρῳ κινηθέντες φιλοσοφίᾳ, δυνάμει τὸν περὶ θεοῦ διὰ πίστεως παρειλήφαμεν λόγον, αὐτουργῷ σοφίᾳ πεπαιδευμένοι. ὃ δὲ μεθ’ ἑτέρου ποιεῖ, ἀτελὲς ὂν καθ’ αὑτὸ ἐνεργεῖν, συνεργόν φαμεν καὶ συναίτιον ἀπὸ τοῦ δὺν αἰτίῳ αἴτιον ὑπάρχειν ἢ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑτέρῳ συνελθὸν αἴτιον γίγνεσθαι ὠνομασμένον, καθ’ ἑαυτὸ δὲ μὴ δύνασθαι τὸ ἀποτέλεσμα τὸ κατ’ ἀλήθειαν παρέχειν. καίτοι καὶ καθ’ ἑαυτὴν ἐδικαίου ποτὲ καὶ ἡ φιλοσοφία τοὺς Ἕλληνας, οὐκ εἰς τὴν καθόλου δὲ δικαιοσύνην, εἰς ἣν εὑρίσκεται συνεργός(καθάπερ καὶ ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ δεύτερος βαθμὸς τῷ εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον ἀνιόντι καὶ γραμματιστὴς τῷ φιλοσοφήσοντι), οὐδ’ ὡς κατὰ τὴν ἀφαίρεσιν αὐτῆς ἤτοι ἐλλείπειν τῷ καθόλου λόγῳ ἢ ἀναιρεῖσθαι τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ἐπεὶ ἡ ὄψις συμβάλλεται καὶ ἡ ἀκοὴ καὶ ἡ φωνὴ πρὸς ἀλήθειαν, νοῦς δὲ ὁ γνωρίζων αὐτὴν προσφυῶς. ἀλλὰ τῶν συνεργῶν τὰ μὲν πλείονα, τὰ δ’ ἐλάσσονα προσφέρεται δύναμιν. ἡ γοῦν σαφήνεια συνεργεῖ πρὸς τὴν παράδοσιν τῆς ἀληθείας καὶ ἡ διαλεκτικὴ πρὸς τὸ μὴ ὑποπίπτειν ταῖς κατατρεχούσαις αἱρέσεσιν. αὐτοτελὴς μὲν οὖν καὶ ἀπροσδεὴς ἡ κατὰ τὸν σωτῆρα διδασκαλία, δύναμις οὖσα καὶ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ, προσιοῦσα δὲ φιλοσοφία ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ οὐ δυνατωτέραν ποιεῖ τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ἀλλ’ ἀδύνατον παρέχουσα τὴν κατ’ αὐτῆς σοφιστικὴν ἐπιχείρησιν καὶ διακρουομένη τὰς δολερὸς κατὰ τῆς ἀληθείας ἐπιβουλὰς φραγμὸς οἰκείως εἴρηται καὶ θριγκὸς εἶναι τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος. καὶ ἣ μὲν ὡς ἄρτος ἀναγκαία πρὸς τὸ ζῆν, ἡ κατὰ τὴν πίστιν ἀλήθεια· ἡ προπαιδεία δὲ προσοψήματι ἔοικεν καὶ τραγήματι, δείπνου δὲ λήγοντος γλυκὺ τρωγάλιον κατὰ τὸν Θηβαῖον Πίνδαρον. ἄντικρυς δὲ ἐξεῖπεν ἡ γραφή· πανουργότερος ἔσται ἄκακος συνίων, ὁ δὲ σοφὸς δέξεται γνῶσιν. καὶ ὁ μὲν ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ λαλῶν τὴν δόξαν τὴν ἰδίαν ζητεῖ, φησὶν ὁ κύριος, ὁ δὲ ζητῶν τὴν δόξαν τοῦ πέμψαντος αὐτὸν ἀληθής ἐστι καὶ ἀδικία οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐτῷ. ἔμπαλιν οὖν ἀδικεῖ ὁ σφετερισάμενος τὰ βαρβάρων καὶ ὡς ἴδια αὐχῶν, τὴν ἑαυτοῦ δόξαν αὔξων καὶ ψευδόμενος τὴν ἀλήθειαν. οὗτος κλέπτης ὑπὸ τῆς γραφῆς εἴρηται. φησὶ γοῦν· υἱέ, μὴ γίνου ψεύστης· ὁδηγεῖ γὰρ τὸ ψεῦσμα πρὸς τὴν κλοπήν. ἤδη δὲ ὁ κλέπτης ὅπερ ὑφελόμενος ἔχει ἀληθῶς κἂν χρυσίον ᾖ κἂν ἄργυρος κἂν λόγος κἂν δόγμα. ἐκ μέρους τοίνυν, ἃ κεκλόφασιν, ἀληθῆ μέν, στοχαστικῶς δὲ καὶ ταῖς τῶν λόγων ἀνάγκαις ἴσασι. μαθητευθέντες οὖν καταληπτικῶς ἐπιγνώσονται.
pass_a_gloss: But just as the many people who pull the ship do not give many reasons, but one reason from many, for the ship is not pulled by each individual, but by all together, so also philosophy, being a search for truth, is taken hold of, not being a cause of attainment, but a cause and co-worker with other things. Perhaps also what is co-causal is causal. Just as, when there is one happiness, the many virtues are causes, and just as the sun and fire and bath and clothing warm, so also, when there is one truth, many things are taken hold of for the search of it, and the discovery is through the Son. If then we consider, virtue is one in power, but it is called prudence in these things, and temperance in these, and courage or justice in these. In the same way, when there is one truth, in geometry it is geometric truth, in music it is musical truth, and in correct Greek philosophy it would be truth. But the only sovereign truth is that which is imparted by the Son of God, and we are taught by Him. We say that just as one drachma given to the shipowner is called naulon, and to the tax collector it is called telos, and to the customs officer it is called enoikion, and to the teacher it is called misthos, and to the seller it is called arrabon, so also each virtue or truth, called by the same name, is a cause of its own effect. But living a happy life happens through the use of these things together, not because we are happy with names, but when we call the right life happiness, and the one who has adorned his soul with virtue happy. If philosophy is also taken hold of from afar for the discovery of truth, extending through different efforts to the knowledge that is near to us, yet it is taken hold of by one who endeavors to attain knowledge logically. But Greek truth is separated from our truth, even if it has shared the same name. And it is greater in the magnitude of knowledge, and in demonstration, and in divine power, and in similar things, for we are taught by God, and we learn sacred writings from the Son of God. Whence it also moves our souls differently, but with different teaching. If we must distinguish ourselves from those who love knowledge, saying that philosophy is co-causal and co-worker for the true attainment, being a search for truth, we will confess it as a preparation for knowledge, not setting the co-causal as a cause, nor the co-worker as a holder, nor as one without which philosophy is not possible, since almost all people, without Greek encyclical education and philosophy, and some even without writings, having been moved by divine and barbarian philosophy, have received the word about God through faith, being self-taught in wisdom. But what does something with another, being incomplete in itself, we call a co-worker and co-causal, from the fact that it has a cause or becomes a cause when it comes together with another, but in itself it is not able to provide the true effect. And yet philosophy has justified the Greeks by itself at some time, not to general justice, to which it is found to be a co-worker, just like the first and second step to the one who ascends to the higher, and the grammarian to the one who philosophizes, nor as if the absence of it would lack the general word or destroy the truth, since sight and hearing and voice contribute to truth, and the mind that knows it is innate. But of the co-workers, some contribute more power, and some less. For clarity co-operates for the transmission of truth, and dialectic for not falling into the heresies that pursue. The teaching through the Savior is then self-sufficient and without need, being the power and wisdom of God, but Greek philosophy, when it comes, does not make truth more powerful, but provides the sophistical effort that is unable to attain it, and it is a fence that rightly repels the cunning plots against the truth. And the truth according to faith is like bread, necessary for living, but philosophy is like a prologue and a trifle, a sweet after-dinner snack, as the Theban Pindar says. But the scripture has spoken clearly: the cunning person will be innocent, understanding, and the wise person will accept knowledge. And the one who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, the Lord says, but the one who seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true, and there is no unrighteousness in him. On the contrary, the one who has taken the things of the barbarians as his own, and boasts about them, and increases his own glory, and lies about the truth, does wrong. This person is called a thief by the scripture. For it says: my son, do not become a liar, for lying leads to theft. And the thief, what he has stolen, he really has, whether it is gold or silver or word or doctrine. Therefore, from the part that they have stolen, they know the truth, but in a conjectural way, and they know the necessities of words. Having been taught in a attainable way, they will know by recognition.

choices.why: the verb συλλαμβάνεται is in the passive voice, indicating that philosophy is being taken hold of
the phrase κατὰ τὸν σωτῆρα indicates the means by which something is done
the adjective ἀδύνατον means unable or powerless
the adjective συνώνυμος means having the same name
the adjective αὐτουργῷ means self-taught or self-sufficient

pass_b_english: Just as the many people who pull a ship do not offer many reasons for its movement, but one reason arising from many -- for no single individual pulls the ship, but they do so together -- so also philosophy, since it is a search for truth, is grasped not as a cause of attainment but as a cause and co-worker together with other things; indeed, what is co-causal may itself be called causal. (Proverbs 30:32) Just as, when happiness is one, many virtues serve as causes, and just as the sun, fire, a bath, and clothing all warm us, so also, when truth is one, many things are grasped for the sake of seeking it, and the discovery of it comes through the Son. If we consider the matter, virtue is one in power, yet it happens to be called prudence in some contexts, temperance in others, and courage or justice in still others; in the same way, though truth is one, in geometry it is geometric truth, in music it is musical truth, and in correct Greek philosophy it would be Greek truth. But the only sovereign truth, which cannot be resisted, is that which we are taught by the Son of God. We say this is like a single drachma given to a shipowner being called passage money, to a tax collector being called a tax, to an innkeeper being called rent, to a teacher being called a fee, and to a seller being called earnest money; likewise, each virtue or truth, though called by the same name, is a cause of its own proper effect. Living well, however, comes about through the combined use of these things -- not because we find happiness in mere names, but when we call the right life happiness and call the one who has adorned his soul with virtue happy. Even if philosophy is grasped from afar for the discovery of truth, stretching through various efforts toward the knowledge that touches us closely, it is nonetheless grasped by the one who strives to attain knowledge by reasoning. Yet Greek truth is separated from our truth, even if it has shared the same name; ours is greater in the magnitude of knowledge, in the authority of demonstration, in divine power, and in similar respects, for we are taught by God, truly sacred, learning the Scriptures from the Son of God. From this source our teaching moves souls differently, not in the same way, but with a different instruction. (John 7:18)

If we must distinguish ourselves from contentious people, we will say that philosophy is co-causal and a co-worker for the true attainment, since it is a search for truth; we will confess it as a preparation for knowledge, not treating the co-causal as a cause, nor the co-worker as self-sufficient, nor as something without which philosophy would be impossible. For almost all people, without Greek encyclical education and philosophy -- and some even without letters -- having been moved by the divine and barbarian philosophy, have received the word concerning God through faith, educated by a self-working wisdom. We call that which works with another, being incomplete for working by itself, a co-worker and co-causal -- whether because it has power as a cause or because it becomes a cause by joining with another -- but by itself it is not able to supply the true result. And yet philosophy did once justify the Greeks by itself, though not to universal justice, to which it is found to be a co-worker -- just as the first and second step serve the one ascending to the upper room, and the grammarian serves the one who will philosophize -- nor as if its absence would make the universal account lacking or would destroy the truth, since sight and hearing and voice contribute to truth, and the mind that knows it is naturally fitted to do so. But among co-workers, some contribute more power, some less; clarity co-operates for the transmission of truth, and dialectic for not falling into the heresies that press upon us. The teaching through the Savior is therefore self-sufficient and without need, being the power and wisdom of God; but Greek philosophy, when it comes alongside, does not make the truth more powerful, but rather supplies a fence that fittingly repels the cunning plots against the truth and renders the sophistical assault against it impossible. The truth according to faith is like bread, necessary for life; philosophy is like a side dish and a delicacy, a sweet snack at the end of a dinner, as the Theban Pindar says. Scripture has spoken outright: 'The cunning person will be innocent, understanding, and the wise person will accept knowledge.' And 'the one who speaks from himself seeks his own glory,' says the Lord, 'but the one who seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true, and there is no unrighteousness in him.' Therefore, the one who has appropriated the things of the barbarians as his own and boasts of them as his own, increasing his own glory and lying about the truth, does wrong. This person is called a thief by Scripture. For it says, 'My son, do not become a liar, for lying leads to theft.' And the thief truly possesses what he has stolen, whether it is gold or silver or word or doctrine. From the part they have stolen, therefore, they know the truth, but conjecturally and according to the necessities of words. Having been discipled in an attainable way, they will come to know by recognition.
notes: The text is a philosophical discussion about the relationship between philosophy and truth, and how they relate to the teachings of the Savior.
